entities.summary:
The Iron Guard, founded in 1927, emerged as a prominent Romanian ultranationalist movement, significantly influencing the sociopolitical landscape of Romania until its dissolution in 1945. Centered in Bucharest, it sought to establish a fascist regime rooted in Orthodox Christianity and Romanian nationalism. Figures such as Corneliu Zelea Codreanu, the movement's charismatic leader, played a crucial role in its rise, rallying support through a mix of anti-communist, anti-Semitic, and nationalist rhetoric.

The Iron Guard's activities were marked by violent actions against perceived enemies, including Jews and political opponents. Between 1930 and 1941, the movement gained considerable traction, even participating in the Romanian government during the National Legionary State under General Ion Antonescu. Notably, the Iron Guard instigated a series of violent pogroms, such as the Bucharest pogrom in 1941, which resulted in the deaths of numerous Jewish citizens and further entrenched the idea of ethno-national superiority within Romanian society.

The legacy of the Iron Guard is complex, as it not only heightened nationalist sentiment in Romania but also laid the groundwork for future extremist ideologies in Eastern Europe. Its influence persisted beyond its official dissolution, echoing in the rise of neo-fascist groups and nationalist sentiments in contemporary Romania. The movement's violent history serves as a cautionary tale against the dangers of extremism and intolerance, illustrating how quickly political movements can devolve into acts of terror.

As historian Lucian Boia noted, 'The Iron Guard was not merely an aberration but a reflection of deep-seated socio-political frustrations in Romania.' This highlights the enduring impact of the Iron Guard's ideology, which continues to resonate in various forms within the Romanian political discourse today.
